extra_text.L8|16: Beta blockers. Demand table (drug class, then effect on heart rate, contractility, systolic wall tension as systolic blood pressure and as left ventricular volume). Beta blockers: heart rate decreased (two arrows down), contractility decreased, systolic blood pressure decreased, left ventricular volume increased. Dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (DHP CCB): heart rate increased, contractility unchanged or decreased, systolic blood pressure decreased (two arrows down), left ventricular volume unchanged or decreased. Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (NDHP CCB): heart rate decreased, contractility decreased, systolic blood pressure decreased, left ventricular volume unchanged or decreased. Nitrates: heart rate increased, contractility blank, systolic blood pressure decreased, left ventricular volume decreased (two arrows down).

extra_text.L8|26: Mechanism figure. Nitrates (nitric oxide) stimulate conversion of GTP to cGMP, which activates protein kinase G and lowers cytosolic calcium, causing smooth muscle relaxation, vasodilation and lower blood pressure. PDE5 breaks cGMP down to inactive GMP. Sildenafil, tadalafil and vardenafil inhibit PDE5. Figure: drug interaction between type 5 PDE inhibitors and nitrates.
extra_text.L8|34: Antianginals and comorbid conditions. Co-morbidity, first line therapy, alternatives, avoid. Hypertension: first line beta blocker, alternative non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker (NDHP). Prior myocardial infarction: first line beta blocker, avoid calcium channel blockers. Decreased left ventricular function: first line beta blocker, alternative amlodipine, avoid other calcium channel blockers. Bradycardia or atrioventricular block: first line dihydropyridine (DHP), alternative long-acting nitrate, avoid non-dihydropyridines and beta blockers. Diabetes: first line non-dihydropyridine, alternatives long-acting nitrate and cardioselective beta blocker, avoid non-cardioselective beta blocker. Asthma: first line non-dihydropyridine and cardioselective beta blocker, avoid non-cardioselective beta blocker.

rows.moa: Inhibit RNA (ribonucleic acid)-dependent protein synthesis at the 50S ribosome (block transpeptidation), so no protein is made and the bacteria die.
rows.indications: Bacterial conjunctivitis. Erythromycin ointment is the most common and is soothing on an inflamed eye; it is also used to prevent ophthalmia neonatorum. Azithromycin costs more but needs fewer doses.
rows.contraindications: None listed; no drug interactions.
rows.adverse: Eye irritation; hypersensitivity.
rows.warning: None stressed.
verify: Inhibits RNA-dependent protein synthesis at the 50S ribosome
Erythromycin is soothing on the inflamed eye

rows.moa: Inhibit DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) gyrase and topoisomerase IV, so supercoiled DNA cannot relax and the DNA breaks (double-stranded breaks).
rows.indications: Conjunctivitis and corneal ulcers. Preferred for corneal ulcers and for Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Preferred for conjunctivitis in contact lens wearers once keratitis is ruled out. Expensive, with frequent dosing.
rows.contraindications: None listed. Caution: rule out keratitis first in a contact lens wearer; emerging resistance; no interactions when given in the eye.
rows.adverse: Ocular irritation; white precipitate (ciprofloxacin, about 17%); unpleasant taste after instillation.
rows.warning: Preferred for corneal ulcers and Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
verify: Preferred for corneal ulcers or Pseudomonas aeruginosa
Preferred for conjunctivitis in contact lens wearers once keratitis is ruled out
ocular irritation, white precipitate (ciprofloxacin ~17%), unpleasant taste after instillation
Preferred for corneal ulcers or Pseudomonas aeruginosa

rows.moa: Bind the 30S ribosomal subunit and interfere with bacterial protein synthesis.
rows.indications: Conjunctivitis (solutions every 2 to 4 hours; ointment 2 to 3 times a day).
rows.contraindications: None listed; no clinically significant interactions.
rows.adverse: Ocular irritation; corneal ulceration; reactive keratoconjunctivitis (with several days of use).
rows.warning: Reactive keratoconjunctivitis after several days of use; corneal ulceration is also listed.
verify: interferes with bacterial protein synthesis by binding to 30S subunits
ocular irritation, corneal ulceration, reactive keratoconjunctivitis (with several days use)
corneal ulceration, reactive keratoconjunctivitis (with several days use)

rows.class: Other topical antibacterials (sulfonamide, polypeptide, folate antagonist plus polymyxin)
rows.moa: Sulfacetamide: blocks folic acid synthesis (antagonizes PABA (para-aminobenzoic acid)). Bacitracin: blocks cell wall synthesis. Trimethoprim: blocks folic acid reduction; polymyxin B: binds membrane phospholipids, so cell contents leak.
rows.indications: Bacterial conjunctivitis (all three). Polytrim (trimethoprim with polymyxin B) is a solution; sulfacetamide comes as ointment or solution; bacitracin as an ointment.
rows.contraindications: Sulfacetamide: avoid in patients with a sulfonamide allergy. Bacitracin and Polytrim: no clinically significant interactions.
rows.adverse: Ocular irritation (all three); sulfacetamide also causes allergic reactions.
rows.warning: Sulfacetamide: avoid in any patient with a sulfonamide allergy.
verify: inhibiting folic acid synthesis through antagonism of PABA
preventing transfer of mucopeptides into the growing cell wall
Inhibits reduction of folic acid to tetrahydrofolate
binds to phospholipids on bacterial cytoplasmic membranes
avoid in patients with a sulfonamide allergy
avoid in patients with a sulfonamide allergy

rows.class: Antivirals for herpes simplex and herpes zoster eye disease
rows.moa: Trifluridine inhibits thymidylate synthetase and is built into viral DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) in place of thymidine, so viral replication stops. Mechanism not given for the other three.
rows.indications: Trifluridine (topical): herpes simplex keratitis and keratoconjunctivitis. Acyclovir: herpes zoster ophthalmicus, herpes simplex iridocyclitis. Valacyclovir, famciclovir (oral): herpes simplex keratitis, herpes zoster ophthalmicus.
rows.contraindications: None listed. No antiviral is used for viral conjunctivitis caused by adenoviruses; it is self-limited.
rows.adverse: Trifluridine: ocular irritation, punctate keratopathy (pinpoint corneal damage), hypersensitivity.
rows.warning: Adenoviral conjunctivitis gets no antiviral: treat symptoms only.
verify: inhibiting thymidylate synthetase and incorporating into viral DNA in place of thymidine
No antiviral agents for viral conjunctivitis caused by adenoviruses
Adverse effects: ocular irritation, punctate keratopathy
No antiviral agents for viral conjunctivitis caused by adenoviruses
treated with symptomatic relief of irritation

rows.moa: Ganciclovir competitively inhibits binding of deoxyguanosine triphosphate to DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) polymerase, blocking viral DNA synthesis. Mechanism not given for the others.
rows.indications: Cytomegalovirus retinitis: ganciclovir (intravenous, oral or intravitreal implant), valganciclovir (oral), foscarnet (intravenous or intravitreal), cidofovir (intravenous). Ganciclovir (Zirgan): herpetic keratitis.
rows.contraindications: None listed.
rows.adverse: Ganciclovir (Zirgan): ocular irritation, punctate keratitis.
rows.warning: Systemic ganciclovir, valganciclovir, cidofovir and foscarnet carry an FDA (Food and Drug Administration) boxed warning (bone marrow suppression, kidney injury, seizures with foscarnet); not stated in the lecture.
verify: competitively inhibiting the binding of deoxyguanosine triphosphate to DNA polymerase
Adverse effects: ocular irritation, punctate keratitis

rows.moa: Natamycin binds sterols and raises fungal cell membrane permeability. Mechanism not given for amphotericin B or the imidazoles.
rows.indications: Natamycin (the only commercially available ophthalmic antifungal): conjunctivitis, keratitis (Aspergillus, Candida, Fusarium and others). Amphotericin B and the imidazoles: yeast and fungal keratitis, endophthalmitis.
rows.contraindications: None listed.
rows.adverse: Natamycin: ocular irritation.
rows.warning: Oral ketoconazole carries an FDA (Food and Drug Administration) boxed warning (liver injury; QT prolongation with interacting drugs); systemic itraconazole and amphotericin B also carry boxed warnings; not stated on the ocular antifungal slide. Risk factors for fungal eye infection: trauma, chronic surface disease, contact lenses, immunosuppression (including topical steroids).
verify: increases cell membrane permeability in fungi by binding to sterol
conjunctivitis, keratitis caused by Aspergillus, Candida, Cephalosporium, Fusarium, and Penicillium
Yeast and fungal keratitis and endophthalmitis

rows.moa: Inverse agonists at the histamine-1 (H1) receptor, still competitive with histamine: decrease capillary dilation, itch and swelling.
rows.indications: Ocular allergy. Dosed 1 to 2 times a day; onset within minutes; allow two weeks to judge full effect. Typically preferred over mast cell stabilizers.
rows.contraindications: None listed; no significant drug interactions.
rows.adverse: Ocular irritation; headache; increased ocular dryness.
rows.warning: Preferred over mast cell stabilizers: onset within minutes.
verify: Decrease capillary dilation, decrease itch, decrease swelling
Allow two weeks of therapy to assess full efficacy
Adverse effects: ocular irritation, headache, increased ocular dryness

rows.moa: Inhibit mast cell degranulation, limiting release of histamine, tryptase and prostaglandin D2; also dampen mediator release from basophils, eosinophils and neutrophils.
rows.indications: Predictable seasonal allergies in patients who do not tolerate other therapies. Full effect takes 5 to 14 days.
rows.contraindications: None listed. Limitation: not useful for acute symptoms (slow onset).
rows.adverse: Ocular irritation; unpleasant taste; headache.
rows.warning: NOT for acute symptoms: 5 to 14 days to full effect, and often four-times-daily dosing.
verify: May be useful for patients with predictable seasonal allergies who don't tolerate other therapies
Adverse reactions: ocular irritation, unpleasant taste, headache

rows.moa: Vasoconstrictor that activates postjunctional alpha-adrenergic receptors on blood vessels, decreasing conjunctival edema (pheniramine adds an antihistamine). Systemically they target alpha-2 receptors.
rows.indications: Decreases conjunctival swelling (edema); over-the-counter; good for under 2 weeks.
rows.contraindications: Not for prolonged use. If no improvement in 72 hours, stop and see a provider (it could be something more serious). Accidental ingestion matters: systemically these act on alpha-2 receptors.
rows.adverse: Rebound hyperemia after prolonged use and stopping.
rows.warning: Rebound hyperemia with prolonged use: limit to under 2 weeks (a key counseling point).
verify: Vasoconstrictor activates postjunctional alpha-adrenergic receptors on blood vessels
Good for short term use (< 2 weeks)
If no improvement in 72 hours, discontinue and see a provider
What does this mean for accidental ingestions?
Prolonged use leads to rebound hyperemia after discontinuation
Prolonged use leads to rebound hyperemia after discontinuation (great counseling point)

rows.moa: Block cyclooxygenase, so arachidonic acid is not converted to prostaglandins and thromboxanes (pro-inflammatory mediators).
rows.indications: Postoperative inflammation and pain; allergic conjunctivitis.
rows.contraindications: None listed. Not routinely recommended for conjunctivitis.
rows.adverse: Lacrimation; keratitis; increased eye pressure; ocular irritation.
rows.warning: Not routinely recommended for conjunctivitis.
verify: Inhibits conversion of arachidonic acid to prostaglandins and thromboxanes
Adverse reactions: lacrimation, keratitis, IOP increase, ocular irritation

rows.moa: Suppress the late-phase allergic reaction: inhibit phospholipase A2, so fewer arachidonic acid-derived inflammatory mediators; also inhibit fibrin and collagen deposition (less scarring).
rows.indications: Severe ocular allergy; anterior uveitis; external eye inflammatory disease; inflammation after ocular surgery. Given topically or intraocularly.
rows.contraindications: Generally reserved for refractory symptoms, limited to under 2 weeks. Cautions: infection, corneal ulcers, glaucoma and raised eye pressure, cataract, delayed wound healing.
rows.adverse: Cataract; raised eye pressure (more with a family history) and glaucoma; infection (decreased immune function); delayed wound healing; corneal ulcers.
rows.warning: Limit to under 2 weeks. Soft steroids (fluorometholone, loteprednol, rimexolone) carry a lower risk of raised eye pressure.
verify: Elevated IOP (more with family history), glaucoma

rows.moa: Hypotonic or isotonic solutions containing electrolytes, surfactants and thickeners; the thickeners increase time in the cul-de-sac.
rows.indications: Dry eye (alteration of the precorneal tear film and ocular surface). Many are over-the-counter.
rows.contraindications: None listed.
rows.adverse: None listed.
rows.warning: Treat the underlying disease first (for example Sjogren syndrome, rheumatoid arthritis, vitamin A deficiency).
verify: Hypo/isotonic solutions containing electrolytes, surfactants, thickeners (increases time in cul-de-sac)
Many conditions affect precorneal tear film

rows.moa: Inhibits production and release of interleukin-2, so less T cell activation: fewer inflammatory markers in the lacrimal gland and more tear production.
rows.indications: Chronic dry eye associated with inflammation (keratoconjunctivitis sicca); improves vision and comfort.
rows.contraindications: None listed; no drug interactions.
rows.adverse: Ocular burning (17%); foreign body sensation; blurred vision.
rows.warning: None stressed.
verify: inhibits production and release of interleukin II
Decreased inflammatory markers in lacrimal gland
chronic dry eye associated with inflammation (keratoconjunctivitis sicca)
ocular burning (17%), foreign body sensation, blurred vision

rows.moa: Analogs of prostaglandin F2-alpha: bind prostaglandin receptors and lower eye pressure by increasing aqueous outflow (exact mechanism unclear).
rows.indications: Glaucoma and ocular hypertension: first-line, the most commonly used glaucoma drugs, once-daily dosing.
rows.contraindications: None listed. Do not exceed once-daily dosing: more frequent dosing inhibits the pressure-lowering effect.
rows.adverse: Conjunctival hyperemia; ocular irritation; changes in eyelash length and iris color. Limited systemic side effects.
rows.warning: Never dose more than once daily (it blunts the effect).
verify: lowers IOP by increasing aqueous outflow
Most commonly used medications for glaucoma
conjunctival hyperemia, ocular irritation, changes in eyelash length and iris color

rows.moa: Block beta receptors in the ciliary body epithelium: less catecholamine activation, less cyclic adenosine monophosphate, less aqueous humor production.
rows.indications: Glaucoma and ocular hypertension (second-line; decreases aqueous production). Start with a prostaglandin analog or a beta blocker.
rows.contraindications: Avoid or use cautiously in heart failure, bradycardia, heart block and asthma. Beta-1 selective agents (betaxolol) carry less bronchoconstriction risk in asthma.
rows.adverse: Worsening heart failure; bradycardia; heart block; increased airway resistance (asthma).
rows.warning: Nonselective agents (timolol, carteolol, levobunolol) work better but cause more side effects; betaxolol is beta-1 selective.
verify: blocks beta receptors in ciliary body epithelium
Generally start with a prostaglandin analog or beta blocker
Less risk for causing bronchoconstriction in patient with asthma history
worsening heart failure, bradycardia, heart block, increased airway resistance (asthma)
Adverse reactions: worsening heart failure, bradycardia, heart block, increased airway resistance (asthma)
Nonselective is more efficacious, but more side effects

rows.moa: Alpha-2 agonists: presynaptically decrease catecholamine release, and postsynaptic alpha-2 activation decreases aqueous production; aqueous outflow also increases.
rows.indications: Glaucoma and ocular hypertension (decrease aqueous production and increase outflow).
rows.contraindications: Contraindicated in children under 2 years (central nervous system depression and apnea).
rows.adverse: Ocular irritation; hyperemia (rebound effect); pruritus; allergic conjunctivitis (less common with brimonidine).
rows.warning: Contraindicated in children under 2 years: central nervous system depression and apnea.
verify: decrease catecholamine release leading to decreased aqueous production and increase outflow
Ocular irritation, hyperemia (rebound effect), pruritus, allergic conjunctivitis (less common with brimonidine)

rows.moa: Inhibit carbonic anhydrase in the ciliary body epithelium: less bicarbonate, less fluid transport, lower eye pressure (decreased aqueous production).
rows.indications: Glaucoma and ocular hypertension. Available in combinations (dorzolamide with timolol; brinzolamide with brimonidine) for fewer drops and better adherence.
rows.contraindications: None listed.
rows.adverse: Bitter taste (25%); burning or stinging after administration (33%); allergic conjunctivitis.
rows.warning: None stressed.
verify: inhibits carbonic anhydrase in ciliary body epithelium
bitter taste (25%), burning/stinging after administration (33%), allergic conjunctivitis

rows.moa: Activate muscarinic receptors, causing ciliary muscle contraction that facilitates aqueous outflow.
rows.indications: Glaucoma (increase aqueous outflow). Acetylcholine (Miochol-E) is used in surgical settings.
rows.contraindications: Younger patients are usually intolerant because of visual blurring; poor compliance from side effects and frequent administration.
rows.adverse: Fixed small pupils; myopia; visual disturbances; headaches.
rows.warning: Poorly tolerated by younger patients (visual blurring).
verify: activates muscarinic receptors causing ciliary muscle contraction facilitating aqueous outflow
Younger patients are usually intolerant of miotic therapy due to visual blurring
Poor compliance due to side effects and frequent administration
Adverse reactions: fixed/small pupils, myopia, visual disturbances, headaches
Younger patients are usually intolerant of miotic therapy due to visual blurring

rows.moa: Inhibit sodium influx into the neuron, preventing signal propagation.
rows.indications: Tonometry; foreign body removal; superficial corneal surgery.
rows.contraindications: None listed. Do not write prescriptions for these.
rows.adverse: Hypersensitivity; burning sensation. Eyes stay numb for 10 to 20 minutes with no blink reflex.
rows.warning: No blink reflex for 10 to 20 minutes; do not write prescriptions for these.
verify: inhibit Na influx into the neuron preventing signal propagation
tonometry, foreign body removal, superficial corneal surgery
eyes will remain numb for 10-20 minutes

rows.moa: Antimuscarinics competitively block muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, causing mydriasis. Phenylephrine is an adrenergic receptor agonist that causes mydriasis and is more reactive to light.
rows.indications: Diagnostic use (fundoscopic examination) and uveitis (prevent synechiae, relieve ciliary spasm).
rows.contraindications: None listed.
rows.adverse: Photosensitivity; blurred vision. Phenylephrine: photosensitivity, conjunctival hyperemia.
rows.warning: None stressed.
verify: More reactive to light than antimuscarinics
Used diagnostically (fundoscopic exams, etc.), uveitis (prevent synechiae, relieves ciliary spasm)

rows.moa: Reveals epithelial defects of the cornea and conjunctiva (a stain).
rows.indications: Anterior segment staining; disclosing corneal injury.
rows.contraindications: None listed.
rows.adverse: Hypersensitivity; burning sensation.
rows.warning: None stressed.
verify: reveals epithelial defects of the cornea and conjunctiva
anterior segment staining, disclosing corneal injury

rows.class: Penicillins (first-line for ear, sinus and throat infections)
rows.moa: Not given in this lecture.
rows.indications: Otitis media: high-dose amoxicillin is the mainstay; amoxicillin-clavulanate if severe, resistant, or antibiotics in the past month. Rhinosinusitis: amoxicillin-clavulanate. Group A streptococcal pharyngitis: amoxicillin or one benzathine penicillin G injection.
rows.contraindications: Penicillin allergy: use an alternative (see the next row).
rows.adverse: Not given in this lecture.
rows.warning: Use a rapid strep test before treating pharyngitis: most cases are viral.
verify: Amoxicillin-clavulanate (Augmentin) for severe or resistant disease
if previous antibiotics received in previous month
Use a rapid strep test to prevent over prescribing

rows.class: Alternatives for penicillin allergy or failed therapy (cephalosporins, macrolide, lincosamide, fluoroquinolone)
rows.moa: Not given in this lecture.
rows.indications: Penicillin-allergic: otitis, cefdinir or azithromycin; sinusitis, clindamycin plus cefixime or levofloxacin; pharyngitis, cephalexin, clindamycin or azithromycin. Failed therapy (no better in 3 days; no antibiotics in past 3 months): amoxicillin-clavulanate or cefdinir; may escalate to ceftriaxone.
rows.contraindications: None listed. Up to 50% of Streptococcus pneumoniae are resistant to macrolides.
rows.adverse: Not given in this lecture.
rows.warning: Levofloxacin: FDA (Food and Drug Administration) boxed warning (tendon rupture, nerve damage, myasthenia gravis worsening). Clindamycin: boxed warning (Clostridioides difficile colitis). Not stated in the lecture. Ceftriaxone (intramuscular) is the step-up for failure.
verify: Cefdinir (Omnicef) or azithromycin (Zithromax) for penicillin allergic patients
May escalate to ceftriaxone IM/IV for failed therapy
50% of S. pneumoniae resistant to macrolides
if oral medications are not tolerated
If no antibiotics in past 3 months

rows.class: Otic anti-infectives (with or without a glucocorticoid)
rows.moa: The anti-infective inhibits bacterial growth; the glucocorticoid decreases inflammatory cytokine production.
rows.indications: Otitis media and otitis externa. Ciprofloxacin with dexamethasone (Ciprodex) is expensive; ofloxacin with dexamethasone ophthalmic drops are the alternative.
rows.contraindications: Polymyxin B: not recommended with a ruptured eardrum or ear tubes in place (cochlear damage, hearing loss).
rows.adverse: Neomycin: hypersensitivity. Polymyxin B: cochlear damage and hearing loss.
rows.warning: Neomycin with polymyxin B drops: avoid with a ruptured eardrum or ear tubes (inner ear damage).
verify: not recommended for patients with ruptured TM or tubes in place
not recommended for patients with ruptured TM or tubes in place

rows.moa: Alters fungal cell wall permeability by inhibiting CYP450 (cytochrome P450).
rows.indications: Systemic fungal infections.
rows.contraindications: None listed as such. Cautions drawn from the adverse effects: QT prolongation, hepatic toxicity, and CYP3A4 (cytochrome P450 3A4) inhibition, which raises levels of other drugs.
rows.adverse: QTc (corrected QT interval) prolongation; hyperlipidemia; orthostatic hypotension; hepatitis, abnormal liver tests, cirrhosis, hepatic failure.
rows.warning: FDA (Food and Drug Administration) boxed warning for oral ketoconazole: liver injury and QT prolongation with interacting drugs (the boxed warning itself is not stated in the lecture; hepatic failure is).
verify: alters fungal cell wall permeability by inhibiting CYP450
Hepatitis, abnormal LFT, cirrhosis, hepatic failure
Hepatitis, abnormal LFT, cirrhosis, hepatic failure

rows.moa: Binds sterols in the fungal cell membrane, increasing permeability.
rows.indications: Oral candidiasis (oral suspension), for example with inhaled steroids, human immunodeficiency virus infection or chemotherapy.
rows.contraindications: None listed.
rows.adverse: Diarrhea; nausea; stomach pain; vomiting.
rows.warning: None stressed.
verify: binds to sterols in fungal cell membrane increase cell wall permeability

rows.moa: Irreversible, noncompetitive inhibitor of platelets; nonselective for cyclooxygenase-1 and cyclooxygenase-2.
rows.indications: Antiplatelet at the lowest doses; antipyretic-analgesic (fever, pain) at higher doses; anti-inflammatory at the highest of these doses.
rows.contraindications: Bleeding disorders; pregnancy (very low doses may help preeclampsia); children with fever from a viral illness (chickenpox, influenza); do not combine with anticoagulants or other nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs.
rows.adverse: Bleeding; gastrointestinal upset, nausea; hypersensitivity; tinnitus. Overdose (salicylism): hyperventilation, alkalosis, then acidosis, shock, coma, death.
rows.warning: Reye syndrome (children under 15, mortality 50%): no aspirin for a child with fever from a viral illness.
verify: very low doses may be of benefit in hypertensive disorders (pre-eclampsia)
Children with fever associated with viral disease (chicken pox/influenza)
Do not take if taking anticoagulants, aspirin inhibits platelet function
Do not take aspirin and other NSAIDS
Shock, coma, respiratory and renal failure, death

rows.moa: Ibuprofen reversibly inhibits cyclooxygenase-1 and cyclooxygenase-2, decreasing prostaglandin synthesis.
rows.indications: Relief of mild to moderate pain (ibuprofen: anti-inflammatory, analgesic, antipyretic). Naproxen (Aleve): longer half-life, less frequent dosing.
rows.contraindications: Allergy to the product; may exacerbate asthma; avoid under 6 months of age; history of stomach ulcers or perforation; renal dysfunction.
rows.adverse: Gastric or duodenal ulcers, perforation, bleeding; edema and fluid retention; acute renal failure.
rows.warning: Prescription NSAIDs carry an FDA (Food and Drug Administration) boxed warning for cardiovascular events and gastrointestinal bleeding (not stated in the lecture). Ibuprofen lowers ACE (angiotensin-converting enzyme) inhibitor effect and raises lithium and methotrexate levels.
verify: Reversibly inhibits cyclooxygenase 1 and 2, decreased prostaglandin synthesis
Indications: relief mild to moderate pain
Avoid in children < 6 months of age
PMHx of stomach ulcers/perforation, renal dysfunction

rows.moa: Not fully elucidated.
rows.indications: Pain; fever above 100 degrees Fahrenheit.
rows.contraindications: Allergy to the product (the only one listed). Alcohol increases the risk of liver damage (chronic use).
rows.adverse: No notable side effects at therapeutic doses; very well tolerated.
rows.warning: Do not exceed 4 g in 24 hours. Alcohol plus acetaminophen raises the risk of liver damage.
verify: Alcohol & Tylenol can increase risk of liver damage (chronically)
Very well tolerated, no notable side effects at therapeutic doses
Alcohol & Tylenol can increase risk of liver damage

rows.moa: Block histamine-1 receptors: block smooth muscle contraction and rapid vasodilation; decrease secretions, edema, hives and itch. Also antimuscarinic, antiemetic and antiserotonergic.
rows.indications: Allergic reactions (rhinitis, urticaria, insect bites, drug hypersensitivity); motion sickness, nausea and vestibular disturbances; over-the-counter sleep aids; adjunct in anaphylaxis.
rows.contraindications: Additive sedation with other central nervous system depressants or alcohol. Excitation instead of sedation at higher doses (especially in children) and in overdose.
rows.adverse: Sedation (the major effect); gastrointestinal disturbances; dry mouth, urinary retention, blurred vision; dermatitis and photosensitivity with topical use.
rows.warning: Sedation is the major side effect; promethazine has the strongest antimuscarinic action. Promethazine carries an FDA (Food and Drug Administration) boxed warning (tissue injury with injection; fatal breathing depression under age 2); not stated in the lecture.
verify: Block smooth muscle contraction (GI and Bronchial)

rows.contraindications: None listed.
rows.adverse: Not given in this lecture.
rows.warning: Enoxaparin carries an FDA (Food and Drug Administration) boxed warning: spinal or epidural hematoma with neuraxial anesthesia or puncture (not stated in the lecture).
